content: Chronic ear infection refers to the presence of fluid, swelling, or infection behind the eardrum that either does not resolve or recurs frequently, potentially causing long-term or permanent damage to the ear. Symptoms of Chronic Ear Infection: Chronic ear infections often present with less severe symptoms compared to acute infections and may go unnoticed or untreated for extended periods. Symptoms can include: Mild ear pain or discomfort, often described as a sensation of pressure in the ear. Low-grade fever. Irritability or fussiness in young infants. Pus-like drainage from the ear. Hearing loss. These symptoms may persist, come and go, and can affect one or both ears. Causes of Chronic Ear Infection: The Eustachian tube, which connects the middle ear to the back of the throat, normally drains fluid from the middle ear. If this tube becomes blocked, fluid can accumulate, creating an environment for infection. Chronic ear infections may result from: An acute ear infection that does not fully resolve. Repeated episodes of ear infections. The term suppurative chronic otitis is used to describe a condition where the eardrum repeatedly ruptures, drains, or swells in the middle ear or mastoid area without resolution. Risk Factors: Children are more prone to ear infections due to their shorter, narrower, and more horizontal Eustachian tubes compared to adults. Chronic ear infections are less common than acute ear infections. Diagnosis: A healthcare provider will examine the ears, which may reveal: Dullness or redness in the middle ear. Air bubbles or thick fluid in the middle ear. The eardrum sticking to the bones of the middle ear. Fluid draining from the eardrum. A perforation (hole) in the eardrum. The eardrum bulging outward or collapsing inward. Additional tests may include: Cultures of the fluid to identify bacteria, which may be resistant or harder to treat than those in acute infections. CT scans of the head or mastoid to check for infection spread beyond the middle ear. Hearing tests to assess any hearing loss. When to Seek Urgent Medical Care: Contact a healthcare provider if: You or your child show signs of a chronic ear infection. An ear infection does not respond to treatment. New symptoms develop during or after treatment. Treatment Options: Antibiotics may be prescribed if the infection is bacterial. Long-term antibiotics may be required, either orally or intravenously. If there is a perforation in the eardrum, antibiotic ear drops are often used. For infections with a perforated eardrum that are difficult to treat, a diluted acidic solution (e.g., distilled vinegar and water) may be recommended. Surgical interventions may include: Cleaning out (debriding) tissue that has accumulated in the ear. Mastoidectomy to remove infection from the mastoid bone. Repairing or replacing the small bones in the middle ear. Repairing the eardrum. Ear tube surgery to improve drainage. Prognosis: Chronic ear infections typically respond to treatment, but prolonged medication use may be necessary. While not life-threatening, chronic ear infections can cause discomfort, hearing loss, and other serious complications. Possible Complications: Permanent changes to the ear and surrounding bones, such as: Mastoiditis (infection of the mastoid bone behind the ear). Persistent drainage from a perforated eardrum or after ear tube insertion. Cholesteatoma (a cyst in the middle ear). Tympanosclerosis (hardening of tissue in the middle ear). Damage or erosion of the middle ear bones, affecting hearing. Facial paralysis. Inflammation around the brain (epidural abscess) or within the brain. Damage to the balance-regulating part of the ear. Partial or complete hearing loss due to middle ear damage, which may lead to delayed language or speech development, especially if both ears are affected. Permanent hearing loss is rare but becomes more likely with repeated or prolonged infections. Prevention: Prompt treatment of acute ear infections can reduce the risk of developing chronic ear infections. Follow-up examinations after treatment of an ear infection are essential to ensure complete resolution.
